plan.title: How Large Language Models Like ChatGPT Work
plan.description: A clear explanation of how large language models learn to predict the next word and turn that simple skill into conversation. Learn about tokens, training, and why these models can sound sure while being wrong.

beats.narration: ChatGPT can write poems, explain physics and fix code. Yet at its core, it does one simple thing over and over: it guesses the next word.

props.title: How ChatGPT Really Works
props.subtitle: One simple trick behind a very smart-sounding machine

beats.narration: You already know this trick. Your phone suggests the next word as you type. A large language model is that idea, scaled up enormously and trained far more deeply.
First, the text is chopped into small pieces called tokens. A token may be a whole word or just part of one. The model works with these pieces, not with letters.

props.definition: A small piece of text, such as a word or part of a word, that a language model reads and writes.

beats.narration: Next comes training. The model reads huge amounts of text, hides the next token, and tries to guess it. Each wrong guess nudges its internal settings a little.
Those settings are called parameters, and there are billions of them. Together they store patterns of language: grammar, facts, styles, and how ideas tend to connect.

props.text: Billions of parameters store the patterns of language.

beats.narration: The key design is the transformer. It uses a method called attention, which lets the model weigh which earlier words matter most for the word it is choosing now.
When you ask a question, the model predicts one token, adds it to the text, then predicts again. Sentence by sentence, an answer is built one piece at a time.
Raw prediction is not yet a helpful assistant. Developers then fine-tune the model with examples of good answers, and with human feedback, so it follows instructions and stays polite.
This explains a famous flaw. The model aims for text that sounds likely, not text that is checked. So it can state something false with total confidence.
So remember the one idea: a language model learns patterns from text and predicts what comes next. Use it as a powerful helper, and verify anything that matters.

props.text: It predicts the next word, so use it well and verify what matters.
